transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-09 14:00 PDT; Duration: 55 mins; Recorded by Fireflies; Location: zoom
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood CSM); Rajiv Malhotra (ArborBank CISO), Elena Park (Cloud Engineer), Tom Whitaker (Head of Ops), Sara Nguyen (Security Analyst), Ken Ito (Compliance)

[00:00] Maya Thompson: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. We're here to walk through audit logs, retention, and the KMS options — Jordan will take most of the deep dive. Quick intros?
[00:08] Rajiv Malhotra: Rajiv - CISO at ArborBank. Goal is to understand exactly what you capture, how long, and how we can export and lock keys. Also interested in the mapping to our RBAC groups.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Great, thanks Rajiv. High level — Redwood logs admin-activity, API calls, model load events, token issuance and invalidation, SSO events, and system-level errors. We call out actor, timestamp, request payload (redacted where needed), response status, and resource ID.
[00:40] Elena Park: When you say payload is redacted, like, do you redact prompt texts or PII by default?
[00:47] Jordan Lee: Good question. By default we do not store full prompt outputs in audit logs — prompts are sampled for quality debugging only if you opt in for debug traces. PII, we try to redact common patterns in the logging pipeline but we recommend customers enforce client-side masking or use prefix stripping before sending.
[01:05] Sara Nguyen: So where do logs land? In hosted you keep them in Redwood's logging store, but can we stream them out immediately?
[01:12] Priya Anand: Yep. There are three supported patterns: batched S3 export (daily/hourly), near-real-time streaming to customer S3 via Kinesis or direct PutObject, and webhook/Splunk HTTP ingestion for SIEMs. We also have optional BigQuery and Snowflake connectors for analytics.
[01:33] Tom Whitaker: For compliance we need immutable retention for 7 years. Can you set retention per-tenant?
[01:40] Jordan Lee: We support per-customer retention policies; retention enforcement for hosted logs is configurable up to your contract limits. For immutable WORM-style we recommend pushing logs to your S3 with Object Lock enabled — Redwood's streaming export can target a pre-provisioned bucket with role-based write-only permissions.
[01:58] Rajiv Malhotra: And audit trail completeness — do you capture API token creation, deletion, and token usage with token id?
[02:05] Jordan Lee: Yes, token lifecycle events are included: create, revoke, rotate, along with actor and IP. We surface a token hash rather than raw token. Occasionally transcription notes: token hash sometimes shows as token id in older exports.
[02:20] Elena Park: How are logs formatted? JSON lines? CSV? Schema stability?
[02:25] Priya Anand: Streaming logs are ndjson (newline-delimited JSON) with a stable schema for top-level fields: timestamp, actor.id, actor.type, action, resource.type, resource.id, request.meta, response.code, region, request_id. We version the schema — schema v1, v2 noted in a header field. Exports to Splunk/HTTP are JSON payloads; BigQuery connector flattens nested fields.
[02:50] Sara Nguyen: What about encryption at rest and CMEK? We need customer-managed keys for logs stored in S3/Buckets, and additionally to avoid keys in Redwood control plane.
[02:58] Jordan Lee: For hosted exports to your S3, the bucket is in your account so the keys are your responsibility — you can enable SSE-KMS with your CMK. For logs retained in Redwood storage we provide encryption at rest with our keys, and we offer a CMEK option for enterprise customers where a customer-managed key is tied into our envelope encryption. That requires an HSM-backed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and a short onboarding flow.
[03:25] Tom Whitaker: If we use CMEK, does Redwood ever have access to the plaintext?
[03:30] Jordan Lee: No, design is envelope encryption — Redwood has encrypted envelopes but without KMS decrypt permission we cannot access plaintext. We do need a limited service role to write metadata, but the key usage logs remain in your KMS.
[03:44] Rajiv Malhotra: Are audit logs part of your SOC2 scope? Can you provide the latest report?
[03:49] Maya Thompson: Yes, logs and change management are in our SOC2 scope. I'll share the SOC 2 Type II report and the control mapping deck after the call.
[03:57] Rajiv Malhotra: Excellent. And the retention settings — you mentioned policy toggles in the Console?
[04:02] Priya Anand: There is a retention UI in the Console where you can set a global default and per-workspace overrides. For programmatic control we expose admin APIs to set retention in minutes/days/years. When you push to S3, you control retention there as well.
[04:18] Elena Park: SSO integration — we use Okta SCIM for provisioning. Can roles map to Redwood RBAC?
[04:24] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning; you can map Okta groups to Redwood roles like admin, auditor, operator, read-only. We recommend provisioning a read-only audit role for SIEM service accounts.
[04:36] Ken Ito: For legal e-discovery can we export a time-bounded subset of logs?
[04:42] Priya Anand: Absolutely — the export API supports query filters (time range, actor, action, resource type) and you can request a bulk export; we deliver a signed manifest and a downloadable ndjson/CSV bundle to S3 or via secure HTTPS link.
[04:55] Tom Whitaker: Are there rate limits for streaming logs to our SIEM? We use Splunk heavy forwarder and don't want to drop events during spikes.
[05:04] Jordan Lee: Streaming is best-effort but we support backpressure; for high-volume customers we recommend the Kinesis streaming path with durable retry on our side. For Splunk HTTP ingestion we provide a buffering layer; we can coordinate with Splunk HEC token sizing. We also have a throttling policy that is controllable via contract.
[05:26] Rajiv Malhotra: How about RBAC audit logs — do you surface policy changes and permission grants?
[05:31] Priya Anand: Yes, RBAC changes are first-class audit events: role assignment, role creation, permission changes, policy updates. Those events include the before/after delta in the request.meta delta field.
[05:44] Sara Nguyen: If we want to do tamper-evidence, do you provide checksums or signed digests for bundles?
[05:50] Jordan Lee: For exported bundles we can produce SHA256 manifests and sign them with our export key. If you use your S3 with Object Lock and SSE-KMS with a CMK, you get tamper-resistance on your side.
[06:05] Elena Park: Any gotchas for data residency? We have EU-only data rules for some teams.
[06:11] Maya Thompson: You can route logs and inference to region-specific hosts. For hosted customers with sensitive EU data, we place logs in EU buckets and use EU-only processing nodes. If you require on-prem, Redwood Private provides full control.
[06:27] Rajiv Malhotra: A couple of nitty-gritty items — 1) How do you correlate request_id to model inference tokens for later debugging without exposing user data? 2) Are internal admin actions (Redwood ops) logged?
[06:38] Jordan Lee: We correlate using a hashed correlation id included in both traces and audit logs, not the raw token. Internal admin actions are logged and tagged as Redwood-operator; access to those logs is restricted and audited — also part of SOC2 scope.
[06:55] Tom Whitaker: For the POC we need a sample payload. Can you share a sample ndjson file and the schema?
[07:00] Maya Thompson: Yes — Jordan will attach a sample export and the schema.
[07:06] Jordan Lee: I'll include three examples: 1) token lifecycle event; 2) RBAC role change; 3) model load + error event. Note: the transcription sometimes flips words like KMS -> KMSy in older exports, so watch for that in examples.
[07:25] Elena Park: For on-call purposes, is there a realtime alerting hook?
[07:29] Priya Anand: We emit critical audit events to a webhook or SNS for alerting — you can tie that to PagerDuty. We also surface anomalies in Console (unusual spikes in token revokes, etc.).
[07:41] Rajiv Malhotra: Ok, so recap: we want streaming exports to our S3 with Object Lock, CMEK for envelope encryption, RBAC mapping from Okta groups, and a retention policy that preserves logs for 7 years in immutable storage. We also want a sample ndjson and a POC to verify schema mapping to Splunk.
[07:58] Maya Thompson: That's right. I'll send SOC2 and compliance pack. Jordan will send sample payloads and KMS integration doc. We'll follow up with dates for the POC.
[08:10] Ken Ito: One last question — do you retain query logs for admin console views?
[08:15] Jordan Lee: We retain console audit trails — who viewed what, export requests, and admin console queries are tracked as events. Query contents are not stored by default unless debug is enabled.
[08:28] Sara Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks folks.
[08:31] Maya Thompson: Thanks everyone. We'll send the docs and propose POC dates.
[08:35] Meeting end.

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings of acronyms and product names, speaker overlap at 00:40-01:00, some filler words removed by auto-trim. References: compliance pack link (shared post-call), sample export link (to be shared), SOC2 report (to be shared).
